messages.subject: Obtain main effects estimates?
parts:
Hello,

 

I am looking for a way to format the summary() output such that only the main effects are listed (example below) and that would allow me to get estimates and CI’s for the overall effect of each treatment.

 

This could include something like the Anova function from the Car package that works with outputs from packages like ‘nlme’ or ‘lme4’ but not ‘MCMCglmm’ or ‘brms’.

 

I have run this model in ‘brms’:

 

fit10 <- brm(Sum ~ A*B*C + (1|Replicate),

            data = Data,

            autocor = cor_ar(~A|B),

            chains=4, iter=3000, warmup=500, thin=15)

 

Levels:

A-  Integer 9 sampling days: (1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9)

B- Factor with 3 levels: north, mid, south

C- Factor with 3 levels: large, medium, small

 

Obtained output:

 

Population-Level Effects:

                                Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat

Intercept                           0.70      0.93    -1.18     2.62        932 1.00

A                                -0.03      0.04    -0.11     0.04        906 1.00

BMid                            0.13      0.88    -1.63     1.89       1092 1.00

BSouth                         -0.58      0.89    -2.30     1.19       1066 1.00

Clarge                      1.46      0.80    -0.05     3.06       1069 1.00

Cmedium                    3.71      0.81     2.15     5.32       1112 1.01

A:BMid                       -0.01      0.06    -0.12     0.11       1063 1.00

A:BSouth                      0.03      0.06    -0.08     0.14        963 1.00

A:Clarge                 -0.01      0.05    -0.12     0.09       1030 1.01

A:Cmedium               -0.01      0.05    -0.11     0.09       1112 1.01

BMid:Clarge            -1.18      1.16    -3.55     1.04       1112 1.00

BSouth:Clarge          -1.43      1.15    -3.73     0.81       1112 1.00

BMid:Cmedium          -2.34      1.15    -4.63    -0.04       1112 1.00

BSouth:Cmedium        -3.15      1.17    -5.37    -0.93       1058 1.00

A:BMid:Cmedium      -0.01      0.07    -0.16     0.13       1009 1.00

A:BSouth:Cmedium    -0.01      0.07    -0.15     0.13       1024 1.00

Fixed effects:

             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   

(Intercept)  0.444294   0.113699   3.908 9.32e-05 ***

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Obtain main effects estimates?
parts:
There is currently no function to compute "main effects" of categorical predictors in the ANOVA sense. In understand, why users want this type of ANOVA-like summaries, but I am not planning to implement it as it is very specific I believe.

The coefficients you see in the output are much more informative that potential ANOVA-like summaries. To better understand your results, I recommend using the marginal_effects method. For your data, you could use for instance:

conds <- data.frame(C = unique(Data$C))
marginal_effects(fit10, "A:B", conditions = conds)

The output of MCMCglmm you are referring to will be the same in brms. The reason, this example looks different is because a, b, and c are continuous not categorical.

Hi Paul,

 

Thank you for your speedy response and advice!

 

I do agree that the coefficients in the output are more informative than the ANOVA-like summaries, unfortunately, some of the comparisons I am interested are not listed in the table and I therefore do not have estimate, l-95% CI, u-95% CI coefficients for them.

 

Following on from your code using conditions and marginal effects:
conds <- data.frame(C = unique(Data$C))

m<-marginal_effects(fit10, "A:B", conditions = conds)

 

This is a nice visual summary, but how can I extract the Estimate, l-95% CI, u-95% CI coefficients from the marginal effects plot in order to give some justification behind saying a relationship is significant or not?
 
Using the following:
 
str(m)
 
m$’A:B’
 
I can see that the “lower__ and upper__” are provided (defined as: lower and upper bounds of the uncertainty interval of the response, https://rdrr.io/cran/brms/man/marginal_effects.html#heading-0). 
 
Can these be used to create an overall l-95% CI, u-95% CI for the effect of A:B?

 

Thank you!

Kate

parts:
I am sorry, if my answers are not what you hope for, but there is no one global estimate corresponding to the elements of a marginal_effects output.

Instead, say, $A:B contains estimates and intervals for all combinations of levels of A and B, but no single effect in the sense you have in mind.

I generally understand where you come from and what kind of output one would expect after having used ANOVAs,
but I currently don't know how to compute this in a reasonable way.

In classical statistics, all of these effects can an associated F-value, but this is not how it works in Bayesian methods.

That said, I will continue to think about this problem and try to come up with something reasonable.

2017-08-30 12:07 GMT+02:00 Kate Quigley <piensagl...@gmail.com>:

Hi Paul,

Thank you for your persistence.


What about a contrast matrix?


I found the following example here (http://www.flutterbys.com.au/stats/tut/tut7.6b.html) using a MCMC framework:

“We could also setup a contrast matrix to compare every factor combination to every other combination. Of course, many of these comparisons would be of very little value, yet since they come at no statistical cost and virtually no CPU cost, we might as well compute them.”

 

library(multcomp)

dt <- expand.grid(A=gl(2,1,2,lab=c('a1','a2')),B=gl(3,1,3,lab=paste('b',1:3,sep="")))

Xmat <- contrMat(n=rep(1,6), type="Tukey") %*% model.matrix(~A*B, dt)

wch <- ldply(strsplit(rownames(Xmat)," - "),as.numeric)

rownames(Xmat) <- paste(interaction(dt$A,dt$B)[wch[,1]],"-",interaction(dt$A,dt$B)[wch[,2]])

pairwise.comps <- coefs %*% t(Xmat)

adply(pairwise.comps,2, MCMCsum)

 

Would this be feasible in brms?


Cheers,

Kate

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Obtain main effects estimates?
parts:
since A is continuous and B and C are categorical, you could try out the following:

model <- brm(y ~ 0 + B:C + A:B:C, data = dat, <more args>)
summary(model)

This model provides you with one intercept per combination of B and C and one slope of A per combination of B and C. Now, you can easily compare combinations with each other.

For instance

hypothesis(
  model,
  hypothesis = c(
    # compare two intercepts
    "BMid:Cmedium - BMid:Clarge = 0",
    # compare two slopes
    "BMid:Cmedium:A - BMid:Clarge:A = 0"
  )
)

You may amend the names of the coefficients to get other contrasts.

I found the following example here (http://www.flutterbys.com.au/stats/tut/tut7.6b.html) using a MCMC framework:

“We could also setup a contrast matrix to compare every factor combination to every other combination. Of course, many of these comparisons would be of very little value, yet since they come at no statistical cost and virtually no CPU cost, we might as well compute them.”

 

library(multcomp)

dt <- expand.grid(A=gl(2,1,2,lab=c('a1','a2')),B=gl(3,1,3,lab=paste('b',1:3,sep="")))

Xmat <- contrMat(n=rep(1,6), type="Tukey") %*% model.matrix(~A*B, dt)

wch <- ldply(strsplit(rownames(Xmat)," - "),as.numeric)

rownames(Xmat) <- paste(interaction(dt$A,dt$B)[wch[,1]],"-",interaction(dt$A,dt$B)[wch[,2]])

pairwise.comps <- coefs %*% t(Xmat)

adply(pairwise.comps,2, MCMCsum)

On Tue, Aug 29, 2017 at 9:33 PM, Paul Buerkner <paul.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
There is currently no function to compute "main effects" of categorical predictors in the ANOVA sense. In understand, why users want this type of ANOVA-like summaries, but I am not planning to implement it as it is very specific I believe.

The coefficients you see in the output are much more informative that potential ANOVA-like summaries. To better understand your results, I recommend using the marginal_effects method. For your data, you could use for instance:

conds <- data.frame(C = unique(Data$C))
marginal_effects(fit10, "A:B", conditions = conds)

The output of MCMCglmm you are referring to will be the same in brms. The reason, this example looks different is because a, b, and c are continuous not categorical.
